### Assistant

And that makes the origin story quite interesting.

You started with a very narrow question:

> **"Do I need an internship to get good opportunities?"**

The initial search essentially framed the alternatives as **formal internship vs. individual project/open-source/research**. Your thinking then kept expanding the problem:

```text
Need internship?
      ↓
Can I create relevant work instead?
      ↓
Why not let other students work on it?
      ↓
Why not evaluate them by capability?
      ↓
Why not train them?
      ↓
Why not let them bring their own projects?
      ↓
Why not involve multiple faculties?
      ↓
Why not involve faculty and mentors?
      ↓
Why not preserve contributors for life?
      ↓
Why not produce research?
      ↓
Why not accept sponsorship/donations?
      ↓
Why not let validated projects become businesses?
      ↓
Why not operate hybrid/online?
      ↓
                    BRAINSTORM
```

That's a pretty significant conceptual jump from the original question.

## One thing the original search got right—and one thing I'd correct

It was reasonable for the search result to warn that **calling something an "internship" does not automatically make it a formal, institutionally recognized internship**, and that employment/trainee arrangements can have legal implications in Nepal. Nepal's official Labour Act and Labour Rules are indeed the relevant legal starting points. 

But I would **not rely on the search result's specific claim** that a formal internship necessarily requires the particular tripartite arrangement it described without checking the applicable provision and your exact structure. I have not established that claim from the official sources yet.

More importantly, **you no longer need to make that legal question the centerpiece of Brainstorm.**

You can build the thing you're describing without pretending it is a conventional corporate internship scheme.

---

# The concept you've arrived at is different

I'd now describe Brainstorm approximately as:

> **A student-led, cross-faculty R&D ecosystem that provides an open-ended pathway for people to develop capability, contribute to or originate research and engineering projects, learn from peers and mentors, produce verifiable work, and potentially take successful work toward publication, open source, products, or ventures.**

And **internship** becomes just one possible downstream outcome.

A researcher might go:

```text
Brainstorm
   ↓
Research contribution
   ↓
Paper
   ↓
Master's / PhD
```

Another:

```text
Brainstorm
   ↓
Engineering project
   ↓
Portfolio evidence
   ↓
Internship / job
```

Another:

```text
Brainstorm
   ↓
Own project
   ↓
Prototype
   ↓
Startup
```

Another:

```text
Brainstorm
   ↓
Contributor
   ↓
Lead
   ↓
Mentor
```

And you:

```text
Personal R&D
      ↓
Brainstorm
      ↓
Researchers
      ↓
Research + projects
      ↓
Network + mentors + sponsors
      ↓
Institutional continuity
```

That's a very different proposition from **"I created unpaid internships to improve my résumé."**

---

## And I think your Cohort 0 idea is the correct starting point

Don't announce the grand ecosystem yet.

Take the few people you already trust.

Teach them selected parts of your knowledge and workflows.

Give them projects appropriate to their current abilities.

Let them use AI heavily.

Observe how they learn, work, verify, collaborate, and improve.

Have them start teaching what they've mastered.

Document what works.

Meanwhile, talk with carefully selected faculty members.

Then Cohort 1 becomes the first **publicly broader manifestation** of a system that has already been tested.

That gives you something extremely valuable that the original Google result could not give you:

**evidence that your alternative actually works.**

---

## And there's a deeper irony

You originally worried:

> **"Maybe I need an internship to become competitive."**

You may end up creating an environment in which **you don't merely gain experience—you create an experience-generating system for other people.**

That's the real potential value of Brainstorm.

But don't skip the hard part: **the organization has to produce genuine work.**

The name, GitHub organization, certificates, titles, faculty connections, notebooks, sponsorships, and future business possibilities are secondary.

The first proof is much simpler:

> **Can Cohort 0 learn from you, independently produce useful work, document it properly, and then teach the next person?**

If yes, the idea has crossed the line from an interesting thought experiment into something you can systematically build.
